packet.headline_seed: Some ancient microbes frozen with Ötzi the Iceman are still growing
packet.description_seed: Ötzi the Iceman, Europe’s most famous mummy, is crawling with microbes, some long dead, some still eking out a living after thousands of years, and some very modern. After he died in the Ötztal Alps, the Copper Age man now known as Ötzi lay alone and forgotten for 5,300 years, until a group of hikers stumbled on his freeze-dried remains in 1991. Since then, he’s received a lot of attention from scientists, who have sequenced his DNA , pored over his last meal and the remains of his gut microbes, and examined his clothes and his broken tools . Today, Ötzi lies in a high-tech resting place at the South Tyrol Museum of Archaeology in Italy, where, it turns out, his body is still home to a handful of cold-adapted yeast species that have probably been with him since just after he died. Slightly morbid souvenirs from the Alps Microbiologist Mohamed S. Sarhan (of the Institute of Mummy Studies at the private Eurac Research center) and his colleagues recently sampled material from Ötzi’s stomach and meltwater from inside his body, swabbed his skin, and even sampled airborne microbes from his frozen storage room and the lab outside it. They also took samples from a block of frozen alpine soil taken from next to Ötzi’s body back in 1991. Read full article Comments

After he died in the Ötztal Alps, the Copper Age man now known as Ötzi lay alone and forgotten for 5,300 years, until a group of hikers stumbled on his freeze-dried remains in 1991. Slightly morbid souvenirs from the Alps Microbiologist Mohamed S. Sarhan (of the Institute of Mummy Studies at the private Eurac Research center) and his colleagues recently sampled material from Ötzi’s stomach and meltwater from inside his body, swabbed his skin, and even sampled airborne microbes from his frozen storage room and the lab outside it. They also took samples from a block of frozen alpine soil taken from next to Ötzi’s body back in 1991. Read full article Comments

Microbiologist Mohamed S. Sarhan (of the Institute of Mummy Studies at the private Eurac Research center) and his colleagues recently sampled material from Ötzi’s stomach and meltwater from inside his body, swabbed his skin, and even sampled airborne microbes from his frozen storage room and the lab outside it. They also took samples from a block of frozen alpine soil taken from next to Ötzi’s body back in 1991. We already know quite a bit about Ötzi’s gut microbes thanks to a 2019 study, but Sarhan and his colleagues wanted the bigger picture. Instead of just sequencing all the microbial DNA they could find on Ötzi, the researchers wanted to understand which species were really part of his ancient one-man ecosystem and which were modern contaminants.

After he died in the Ötztal Alps, the Copper Age man now known as Ötzi lay alone and forgotten for 5,300 years, until a group of hikers stumbled on his freeze-dried remains in 1991. Since then, he’s received a lot of attention from scientists, who have sequenced his DNA, pored over his last meal and the remains of his gut microbes, and examined his clothes and his broken tools. Today, Ötzi lies in a high-tech resting place at the South Tyrol Museum of Archaeology in Italy, where, it turns out, his body is still home to a handful of cold-adapted yeast species that have probably been with him since just after he died.

That said, there’s been less attention paid to Ötzi’s microbiome, according to study author Frank Maixner, head of the Institute for Mummy Studies at Eurac Research. Maixner and his team weren’t just interested in identifying the microorganisms preserved inside his body but also those on the surface, which could include microbes inadvertently introduced to Ötzi after he was unearthed. They collected samples from Ötzi and his storage environment at the South Tyrol Museum of Archaeology in Italy for genetic analysis. They also analyzed soil samples from the original site where he was found and samples from Ötzi previously collected in 1992, 2010, and 2019. From all this analysis, they made two major discoveries.

Ötzi the Iceman, Europe’s most famous mummy, is crawling with microbes, some long dead, some still eking out a living after thousands of years, and some very modern.

After he died in the Ötztal Alps, the Copper Age man now known as Ötzi lay alone and forgotten for 5,300 years, until a group of hikers stumbled on his freeze-dried remains in 1991. Since then, he’s received a lot of attention from scientists, who have sequenced his DNA, pored over his last meal and the remains of his gut microbes, and examined his clothes and his broken tools. Today, Ötzi lies in a high-tech resting place at the South Tyrol Museum of Archaeology in Italy, where, it turns out, his body is still home to a handful of cold-adapted yeast species that have probably been with him since just after he died.

Microbiologist Mohamed S. Sarhan (of the Institute of Mummy Studies at the private Eurac Research center) and his colleagues recently sampled material from Ötzi’s stomach and meltwater from inside his body, swabbed his skin, and even sampled airborne microbes from his frozen storage room and the lab outside it. They also took samples from a block of frozen alpine soil taken from next to Ötzi’s body back in 1991.

We already know quite a bit about Ötzi’s gut microbes thanks to a 2019 study, but Sarhan and his colleagues wanted the bigger picture. Instead of just sequencing all the microbial DNA they could find on Ötzi, the researchers wanted to understand which species were really part of his ancient one-man ecosystem and which were modern contaminants.

Sarhan and his colleagues cultured some of the samples, and also put some through a process called shotgun metagenomics, which involves sequencing all the bits of DNA floating around in a sample. Inside Ötzi’s guts, Sarhan and his colleagues—like previous studies—found ancient DNA from a host of bacteria that match what we expect of ancient, “non-Westernized” gut microbiomes. But elsewhere on and in the mummy, the team also found some microbes that weren’t actually dead.

Ötzi is kept in carefully maintained conditions, as close as possible to the glacier that preserved his body for more than 5,000 years. The chamber is a brisk -6º Celsius, with 99 percent humidity carefully maintained by a spray of UV-treated water. [Lähde: Gizmodo]
A relic of humanity’s past isn’t so dormant after all. Research out today shows the remains of Ötzi “the Iceman” are teeming with living microorganisms.

Scientists in Italy conducted an extensive survey of Ötzi, a mummy naturally frozen in a mountain glacier for over 5,000 years. They found ample bacteria and fungi inside and on Ötzi’s body, some of which might have survived for millennia and appear to be active even today under tightly maintained storage conditions. The findings not only illustrate the resilience of microbial life but also suggest we need to be more careful about how these sorts of specimens are preserved once discovered.

“Our comprehensive assessment reveals that the Iceman is not a biologically ‘frozen’ time-capsule but rather a complex ecosystem,” the authors wrote in their paper, published Tuesday in the journal Microbiome.

In 1991, Ötzi was discovered in the Ötztal Alps that straddle the current borders between Italy and Austria. He’s the oldest known glacial mummy ever found and is believed to have died at the age of 45 some 5,300 years ago.

Since his discovery, scientists have learned much about Ötzi’s life and the Copper Age society he was a part of. That includes his last meal and the likely possibility that he was killed via an arrow to his back. The tools he was found with were also sourced from different, sometimes very distant regions, suggesting the existence of a lengthy trade route along that part of Europe.

Genetic Analysis of ‘Ötzi the Iceman’ Reveals Ancient Mummy’s Ancestry

That said, there’s been less attention paid to Ötzi’s microbiome, according to study author Frank Maixner, head of the Institute for Mummy Studies at Eurac Research. Maixner and his team weren’t just interested in identifying the microorganisms preserved inside his body but also those on the surface, which could include microbes inadvertently introduced to Ötzi after he was unearthed.

They collected samples from Ötzi and his storage environment at the South Tyrol Museum of Archaeology in Italy for genetic analysis. They also analyzed soil samples from the original site where he was found and samples from Ötzi previously collected in 1992, 2010, and 2019. From all this analysis, they made two major discoveries.

Ötzi the Iceman has long been treated as a frozen messenger from the Copper Age. But his remains might not be completely preserved in time, a new study suggests.

A team has identified cold-adapted yeasts that could have colonized Ötzi during his glacial deep freeze as well as genetic traces of the gut microbes he died with five millennia ago. The results, published June 3 in Microbiome, suggest the modern microbiome of the remains could affect Ötzi’s preservation.

payload.title: Ötzin muumiosta löytyi yhä eläviä kylmään sopeutuneita mikrobeja
payload.summary: Tutkijat ovat analysoineet Ötzin ruumiista, säilytysympäristöstä ja löytöpaikan maaperästä otettuja näytteitä erottaakseen muinaiset mikrobit nykyaikaisista epäpuhtauksista.
payload.content:
Ötzinä tunnetun jäämiehen muumio kantaa yhä mukanaan mikrobeja, joista osa on kuollut, osa nykyaikaisia tulokkaita ja osa todennäköisesti peräisin ajalta pian hänen kuolemansa jälkeen. Uusissa analyyseissä tutkijat havaitsivat, että Etelä-Tirolin arkeologisessa museossa Italiassa säilytettävässä muumiossa elää yhä pieni joukko kylmään sopeutuneita hiivalajeja.

## Näytteitä ruumiista ja säilytystiloista

Kuparikaudella elänyt Ötzi kuoli Ötztalin Alpeilla noin 5 300 vuotta sitten. Retkeilijät löysivät hänen jäätyneet ja kuivuneet jäännöksensä vuonna 1991. Löydön jälkeen tutkijat ovat selvittäneet muun muassa hänen DNA:taan, viimeistä ateriaansa, suolistomikrobiensa jäänteitä, vaatteitaan ja rikkoutuneita työkalujaan.

Mikrobiologi Mohamed S. Sarhan Eurac Research -tutkimuskeskuksen muumiotutkimuksen instituutista ja hänen kollegansa keräsivät nyt näytteitä Ötzin vatsasta, hänen kehonsa sisältä peräisin olevasta sulamisvedestä ja iholta. Lisäksi he tutkivat ilmassa olevia mikrobeja sekä muumion jäädytetystä säilytyshuoneesta että sen ulkopuolisesta laboratoriosta.

Vertailua varten ryhmä analysoi myös jäätynyttä alppimaata samalta alueelta, josta Ötzi löydettiin vuonna 1991. Mukana oli lisäksi aiemmin Ötzistä kerättyjä näytteitä vuosilta 1992, 2010 ja 2019.

## Tavoitteena erottaa vanha ja uusi

Tutkimuksen keskeinen kysymys ei ollut vain se, mitä mikrobeja Ötzistä löytyy. Tutkijat pyrkivät selvittämään, mitkä lajit kuuluivat muumion muinaiseen mikrobiyhteisöön ja mitkä ovat päätyneet häneen vasta löydön jälkeen esimerkiksi käsittelyn, säilytyksen tai ympäristön kautta.

Frank Maixnerin mukaan Ötzin mikrobiomi on saanut vähemmän huomiota kuin moni muu osa jäämiehen tutkimusta. Siksi tutkijat tarkastelivat sekä ruumiin sisällä säilyneitä mikro-organismeja että pinnalla olevia mikrobeja, joihin voi sisältyä myöhempiä epäpuhtauksia.

Havainnot korostavat, että hyvin säilynyt muumio ei ole vain biologinen aikakapseli, vaan myös muuttuva ympäristö. Ötzin nykyinenkin säilytyspaikka vaikuttaa siihen, millaisia mikrobeja hänen ruumiistaan voidaan löytää, ja siksi muinaisen elämän jälkien erottaminen nykyisistä kontaminaatioista vaatii laajaa vertailua.
summary_bullets: Ötzin muumiosta on löytynyt kylmään sopeutuneita hiivalajeja, jotka saattavat olla peräisin pian hänen kuolemansa jälkeiseltä ajalta.
Tutkijat analysoivat näytteitä muumiosta, säilytystiloista, löytöpaikan maaperästä ja aiemmista tutkimusnäytteistä.
Tavoitteena oli erottaa muinaiseen mikrobiyhteisöön kuuluvat lajit myöhemmistä epäpuhtauksista.

article.summary: Tutkijat ovat analysoineet Ötzin ruumiista, säilytysympäristöstä ja löytöpaikan maaperästä otettuja näytteitä erottaakseen muinaiset mikrobit nykyaikaisista epäpuhtauksista.
article.content:
Ötzinä tunnetun jäämiehen muumio kantaa yhä mukanaan mikrobeja, joista osa on kuollut, osa nykyaikaisia tulokkaita ja osa todennäköisesti peräisin ajalta pian hänen kuolemansa jälkeen. Uusissa analyyseissä tutkijat havaitsivat, että Etelä-Tirolin arkeologisessa museossa Italiassa säilytettävässä muumiossa elää yhä pieni joukko kylmään sopeutuneita hiivalajeja.

## Näytteitä ruumiista ja säilytystiloista

Kuparikaudella elänyt Ötzi kuoli Ötztalin Alpeilla noin 5 300 vuotta sitten. Retkeilijät löysivät hänen jäätyneet ja kuivuneet jäännöksensä vuonna 1991. Löydön jälkeen tutkijat ovat selvittäneet muun muassa hänen DNA:taan, viimeistä ateriaansa, suolistomikrobiensa jäänteitä, vaatteitaan ja rikkoutuneita työkalujaan.

Mikrobiologi Mohamed S. Sarhan Eurac Research -tutkimuskeskuksen muumiotutkimuksen instituutista ja hänen kollegansa keräsivät nyt näytteitä Ötzin vatsasta, hänen kehonsa sisältä peräisin olevasta sulamisvedestä ja iholta. Lisäksi he tutkivat ilmassa olevia mikrobeja sekä muumion jäädytetystä säilytyshuoneesta että sen ulkopuolisesta laboratoriosta.

Vertailua varten ryhmä analysoi myös jäätynyttä alppimaata samalta alueelta, josta Ötzi löydettiin vuonna 1991. Mukana oli lisäksi aiemmin Ötzistä kerättyjä näytteitä vuosilta 1992, 2010 ja 2019.

## Tavoitteena erottaa vanha ja uusi

Tutkimuksen keskeinen kysymys ei ollut vain se, mitä mikrobeja Ötzistä löytyy. Tutkijat pyrkivät selvittämään, mitkä lajit kuuluivat muumion muinaiseen mikrobiyhteisöön ja mitkä ovat päätyneet häneen vasta löydön jälkeen esimerkiksi käsittelyn, säilytyksen tai ympäristön kautta.

Frank Maixnerin mukaan Ötzin mikrobiomi on saanut vähemmän huomiota kuin moni muu osa jäämiehen tutkimusta. Siksi tutkijat tarkastelivat sekä ruumiin sisällä säilyneitä mikro-organismeja että pinnalla olevia mikrobeja, joihin voi sisältyä myöhempiä epäpuhtauksia.

Havainnot korostavat, että hyvin säilynyt muumio ei ole vain biologinen aikakapseli, vaan myös muuttuva ympäristö. Ötzin nykyinenkin säilytyspaikka vaikuttaa siihen, millaisia mikrobeja hänen ruumiistaan voidaan löytää, ja siksi muinaisen elämän jälkien erottaminen nykyisistä kontaminaatioista vaatii laajaa vertailua.

Ötzi the Iceman, Europe’s most famous mummy, is crawling with microbes, some long dead, some still eking out a living after thousands of years, and some very modern. After he died in the Ötztal Alps, the Copper Age man now known as Ötzi lay alone and forgotten for 5,300 years, until a group of hikers stumbled on his freeze-dried remains in 1991. Since then, he’s received a lot of attention from scientists, who have sequenced his DNA , pored over his last meal and the remains of his gut microbes, and examined his clothes and his broken tools . Today, Ötzi lies in a high-tech resting place at the South Tyrol Museum of Archaeology in Italy, where, it turns out, his body is still home to a handful of cold-adapted yeast species that have probably been with him since just after he died. Microbiologist Mohamed S. Sarhan (of the Institute of Mummy Studies at the private Eurac Research center) and his colleagues recently sampled material from Ötzi’s stomach and meltwater from inside his body, swabbed his skin, and even sampled airborne microbes from his frozen storage room and the lab outside it. They also took samples from a block of frozen alpine soil taken from next to Ötzi’s body back in 1991. We already know quite a bit about Ötzi’s gut microbes thanks to a 2019 study, but Sarhan and his colleagues wanted the bigger picture. Instead of just sequencing all the microbial DNA they could find on Ötzi, the researchers wanted to understand which species were really part of his ancient one-man ecosystem and which were modern contaminants.

Since then, he’s received a lot of attention from scientists, who have sequenced his DNA, pored over his last meal and the remains of his gut microbes, and examined his clothes and his broken tools. Today, Ötzi lies in a high-tech resting place at the South Tyrol Museum of Archaeology in Italy, where, it turns out, his body is still home to a handful of cold-adapted yeast species that have probably been with him since just after he died.

That said, there’s been less attention paid to Ötzi’s microbiome, according to study author Frank Maixner, head of the Institute for Mummy Studies at Eurac Research. Maixner and his team weren’t just interested in identifying the microorganisms preserved inside his body but also those on the surface, which could include microbes inadvertently introduced to Ötzi after he was unearthed. They collected samples from Ötzi and his storage environment at the South Tyrol Museum of Archaeology in Italy for genetic analysis. They also analyzed soil samples from the original site where he was found and samples from Ötzi previously collected in 1992, 2010, and 2019. From all this analysis, they made two major discoveries.
